Project Proposal: Dynamic Environmental Health Engine (DEHE)

Transforming Urban Data into Personalized Health Recommendations

Max (Team Gucci!) ·

Challenge: "How can we transform environmental data into personalized recommendations to prevent health risks in everyday life?". Despite the availability of data on air quality, noise levels, and weather conditions, this information is often inaccessible and rarely translated into useful insights for citizens. People with respiratory conditions or other health issues are particularly vulnerable, yet they lack tools that allow them to adjust their behavior based on real-time data.

1. The Problem, In Four Parts

Turning raw sensor data into a genuinely useful piece of personal advice is harder than it looks, for four reasons:

  • Space: Environmental stress varies over different distances, and can have many different effects. E.g. roads make a lot of noise over a short range, while airports cause noise across wider areas. There are many different layers and effects simply from the environment.
  • Time: Risks move through the day, e.g. pollution peaks at rush hour, heat peaks mid-afternoon, and some hazards (a festival, a fire) exist for a few hours and then are gone.
  • Events: A city is never static. There can be events that cause noise, pollution, or mitigation strategies that people will want to find (cool zones, or shelters, etc).
  • The person: The same air is not the same risk for everyone, e.g. somebody with asthma has a different risk profile than a senior citizen or a random person.

A useful tool has to hold all four of these at once: a map, a clock, a live events layer, and a person.

2. My Pitch: the Dynamic Environmental Health Engine

We can build a small working engine that does exactly this for Lisbon, and a live web app to demonstrate it. It has four moving parts:

A. Spatial-Temporal Engine

Builds continuous, hour-by-hour risk layers for Heat, Noise, Air Pollution, and UV across a fine grid of Lisbon, combining physical city features (roads, green space, water, density) with live weather forecasts.

B. Live Event & Policy Layer

Lets a city (or our demo) inject a temporary hazard or mitigation. In the example we've added a music event, an industrial fire, and heat-wave mitigation zones (e.g. public buildings to cool down).

C. Personal Risk Profiles

Turns the same underlying environmental data into a different score for different people, by weighting each hazard according to a vulnerability profile (e.g. respiratory conditions, older adults).

D. A Working Map We Can Unveil

We don't yet know if it will become a full app, but a public website with this information already ticks every challenge box. It's light-weight (Leaflet, GitHub), so everybody can see the demo in action.

Together, these four pieces are less a dashboard and more a living model of the city: it doesn't just report what the air is like, it tells a specific person what to do about it, right now, where they are.

3. How It's Built

[ City Geometry & Weather ] ──► [ Hazard Modelling ] ──► [ Event Layer ] ──► [ Personalization ] ──► [ Web App ]

We're building this in five phases. The proof of concept already runs end-to-end for Lisbon; the phases below describe what's solid and what's next.

For the demo, we're running the engine live for Lisbon over the days of the conference itself — so the risks on screen are the risks in the room, which makes the case for the tool far better than any slide could.

Worth saying plainly: what's built so far is a proof-of-concept of a proof-of-concept. It works end-to-end, but every phase below has a clear next step for making it production-grade.

  • Phase 1 — Data Foundation: pull real city geometry and weather (for 4 days), turn it into a mathematical grid.
  • Phase 2 — Hazard Modelling: turn grid features into physical risk values (°C, dB, µg/m³, UV index) using spatial decay and time-of-day patterns.
  • Phase 3 — Events & Policy: let temporary hazards and mitigations (fires, festivals, cooling centers) reshape the map in real time.
  • Phase 4 — Personalization: turn one shared risk map into a different score and recommendation per person.
  • Phase 5 — Deployment: ship it as a live, lightweight web app anyone can open.

We start from what's already public. On first run, the engine pulls OpenStreetMap geometry for Lisbon (roads, rail, airports, green space, water, urban density, elevation) and caches it locally, since this step is slow and doesn't need repeating.

Those features are polygons and lines; the engine needs numbers on a grid. So everything is rasterized onto a 250m × 250m grid over the city — the same resolution every other phase builds on.

Alongside this, we pull a 5-day weather forecast (temperature, UV, PM2.5, NO2): the Open-Meteo API supports up to 16 days if we want to extend the horizon later, at the cost of larger files. As a further step we can include more weather predictions (e.g. wind speed and direction).

A grid of features isn't a risk map yet — each feature needs an effect size and a reach. An airport, for example, raises noise a lot but over a wide area; dense housing raises it a little but only close by. We model this with a distance-decay function per feature, currently tuned by hand and worth validating against real measurements later (e.g. regressing historical Lisbon weather against known urban heat island effects).

Since one feature can affect several hazards at once (an airport touches noise, heat, and pollution together), every relevant feature is combined into each of the four hazard layers, giving four continuous, physically-real-unit maps of Lisbon.

This is the piece that turns a static model into something a city could actually operate day to day. On top of the physical baseline, the engine accepts a list of time- and place-bound events (e.g. a fire, a concert, a heatwave cooling center) each with its own footprint, magnitude, radius of influence, and active hours. When an event is live, it's blended straight into the grid for exactly its duration; when it ends, the map reverts to baseline with no manual reset needed.

For example, an event in code could look like this:

list(
  id = "montijo_fire_emergency",
  label = "Montijo Airbase Industrial Fire",
  risks = c("pollution", "heat"),
  effect_type = "additive",
  coords = matrix(c(-79000, -106500, -77000, -106500, -77000, -105500,
                     -79000, -105500), ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE),
  magnitude = list(pollution = 85.0, heat = 14.0),
  d0_m = 1500,
  start_time = as.POSIXct("2026-09-29 06:00:00", tz = "UTC"),
  end_time   = as.POSIXct("2026-09-29 22:00:00", tz = "UTC"),
  active_hours = 0:23
)

This is also the natural door into a smart-city ecosystem: the same interface that takes our demo events could just as easily take a live feed from a municipal alert system, a traffic authority, or emergency services — no changes to the engine required, only a new source for the same event format. Fundamentally we don't need to know what the smart-city ecosystem looks like yet (it will be different for each city and system anyway) — we only need to show that our model is modular enough to include these features.

Ideas: we can add traffic, shelters, and other smart-city information as further event types.

The four hazard layers are shared, but no two people should read them the same way. Each user profile (e.g. someone with a respiratory condition, an older adult, a general default) carries its own weighting across Heat, Noise, Pollution, and UV, so the same street corner produces a different score (and a different plain-language recommendation) depending on who's asking.

For the demo we can just highlight different profiles. A real version will eventually improve this further (e.g. individual personal profiles), but the underlying mechanism is the same.

The engine exports each day's grids as compact JSON files, published alongside a self-contained web app (Leaflet.js) to GitHub Pages. There's no server to run and nothing to install: anyone with the link opens it on a phone or laptop, picks a profile, and drags the time slider through the day to see the map, an event timeline, and a live recommendation update in real time.

This is a lot better than the other mathematical-model web-app setups we know: e.g. Shiny, Dash, or Streamlit all become laggy for large models and many simultaneous users. This static-file setup should work for the entire audience at once. Because it's just static files, it's also trivial to embed this same view inside another platform later.

I have made a small POC model that should now work, e.g. showing a map, hazards, events, etc. The spatial features and weather are already automatically downloaded, but the rest is just fictitious dummy data. Link: https://maxlelie.github.io/LisboaPOC/
